strengths: The paper addresses a timely and underexplored question: whether feed-forward 3D foundation models like VGGT internalize universal geometric principles (epipolar geometry, correspondences) or merely rely on learned data priors. This fills a genuine gap in interpretability research for 3D vision models.

The methodological design is sound and multi-faceted: layer-wise probing of the fundamental matrix (Fig. 2), analysis of QK attention space for correspondence matching (Fig. 3), and targeted attention-knockout interventions establishing a causal link (Fig. 4). The progression from correlational evidence to causal intervention follows best practices from mechanistic interpretability.

The emergence of correspondence matching at layers 10-16 preceding the sharp improvement in fundamental-matrix recovery (layers 13-14), combined with targeted interventions showing large Sampson error increases (71.7-118.8 px) versus negligible effects for early/late layers, provides a coherent and convincing narrative.

The supplementary material strengthens the paper considerably: rank-ratio validation of F (Fig. 10), bidirectional correspondence analysis (Fig. 11), progressively more localized interventions (Figs. 13-14) that address the non-locality confound, and additional robustness results across viewpoint configurations (Fig. 17).

The data-prior analysis (occlusions, lighting, symmetry, focal length) is systematic and yields interesting practical findings, e.g., that VGGT 'hallucinates' occluded correspondences rather than ignoring them, and its sensitivity to asymmetric lighting changes that remove shadows.

The paper is honest about its limitations, including the synthetic-data scope, the potential confound of SIFT struggling on texture-less synthetic scenes, and the fact that interventions do not conclusively isolate correspondence matching itself as the causal mechanism.
weaknesses: All experiments are conducted on a small, controlled synthetic ShapeNet/Blender dataset. Some key experiments use very few scenes (e.g., correspondence accuracy averaged over 5 scenes; interventions over 5 scenes; occlusions over 40 scenes). Generalization of the findings to real images, diverse scenes, and more than two views is not demonstrated, which limits the strength of the central claim about VGGT's 'geometric understanding'.

Probing is restricted to the camera token only, motivated by the camera head using the final-layer camera token. The possibility that patch tokens encode epipolar information differently (or earlier) is not examined, so the layer-localization conclusions may be incomplete.

The robustness comparison against classical baselines (SIFT + 8-point + RANSAC, SuperGlue + RANSAC) is partially confounded, as the authors themselves acknowledge: SIFT performs poorly on texture-less synthetic renders, and SuperGlue's high failure rates on synthetic images may not reflect its behavior on natural imagery. The 'superior robustness' claim would be stronger with real-image validation.

The causal claim is appropriately hedged but remains somewhat indirect: knockout of entire attention maps (and even the localized variants in the supplementary) may disrupt other mechanisms co-located in the same heads. The paper's own caveat that 'our interventions were not local enough' means the headline claim of a causal correspondence-to-epipolar link is not fully established.

The concurrent work of Stary et al. [25] on understanding multi-view transformers (DUSt3R variant) substantially overlaps in motivation and methodology; the paper cites it only briefly without a direct comparison or discussion of how findings differ or complement each other.
No mention of code or dataset release, which limits reproducibility of the probing and intervention pipelines despite the synthetic data being straightforward to regenerate.

Some robustness findings (e.g., VGGT being more robust than classical pipelines under occlusion and appearance changes) are largely confirmatory of what the training-augmentation story would predict, reducing the novelty of Section 5 relative to Section 4.

strengths: Timely and well-motivated research question: whether feed-forward 3D foundation models (VGGT) internalize geometric principles (correspondences, epipolar geometry) or rely purely on learned data priors is a question of genuine interest to the community, and interpretability work on geometric 3D models is scarce.

The analysis follows a sensible, layered methodology: probing (Fig. 2), attention-space correspondence analysis (Fig. 3), and then targeted interventions (Fig. 4), progressing from correlational to causal evidence. The supplementary interventions with progressively more localized knockouts (Figs. 12–14) meaningfully strengthen the causal argument.

The controlled synthetic dataset with full ground truth (poses, correspondences, fundamental matrices, symmetric/unique object splits, multiple focal lengths and camera configurations) is a reasonable design choice for mechanistic analysis, and the construction is documented sufficiently for reproducibility.

The paper is honest about what its evidence does and does not show: the discussion and limitations section carefully hedges the causal claim (interventions are not local enough to isolate correspondence matching per se) and acknowledges the synthetic-data confound for classical baselines.

The occlusion/hallucination finding (VGGT partially recovers correspondences for occluded patches rather than ignoring them) is an interesting, practically relevant observation about the model's behavior.

The robustness study (lighting, symmetry/repetition, focal length) with classical and learned baselines provides a useful empirical characterization of where VGGT succeeds and fails (e.g., failure under asymmetric lighting changes).
weaknesses: The scale of the evaluation is very small for the strength of the claims made. The intervention/casual analysis rests on only 5 test scenes; the probing splits use 20/20/5/7 scenes; the occlusion study uses 40 scenes. For a paper whose core contribution is empirical evidence about internal mechanisms, these sample sizes are thin and leave open the possibility that the reported layer-wise transitions and intervention effects are not robust across scenes or object categories.

The study is entirely confined to synthetic ShapeNet renderings of single objects in simple scenes. The paper acknowledges that texture-less synthetic scenes disadvantage SIFT-based baselines, which confounds the 'VGGT is more robust than classical pipelines' conclusion; no real-image validation is attempted, even on a small subset (e.g., a few real pairs with COLMAP ground truth).

The concurrent work of Stary et al. [25] performs a closely related analysis (internal state, layers, correspondences) on DUSt3R-style models. The paper cites it only in passing; a more careful positioning and differentiation of what is new beyond [25] — beyond moving from DUSt3R to VGGT — is needed to establish novelty.

Several main findings are arguably expected: it is unsurprising that a multi-view transformer trained to align views contains correspondence structure in mid-layer global attention, and that this is causally involved in geometry prediction. The paper would be stronger if it uncovered something non-obvious about the mechanism (e.g., how epipolar structure is composed from correspondences, or a surprising failure mode beyond symmetric-lighting ambiguity).

Probing is restricted to the camera token only, justified by the camera head using the final-layer camera token. It is not clear that the camera token is where cross-view geometric information should concentrate; probing patch tokens or the attention outputs would make the 'where is geometry encoded' claim more complete.

The core causal intervention is coarse: zeroing entire weight matrices for layer-head combinations (and in the main result, the whole attention map for all patches) destroys many functions beyond correspondence matching. The more localized interventions appear only in the supplementary and still show a much smaller effect (Fig. 14: 10.2 px increase vs. 118.8 px in Fig. 4), which weakens the headline causal claim as presented in the main text.

Some experimental reporting lacks precision: the correspondence-matching accuracy experiment uses '5 scenes' without variance estimates or confidence intervals anywhere; the definition of 'failure' (Sampson error > 10 px) is somewhat arbitrary; and Figure 5's occlusion results center on one illustrative case with aggregate statistics that are hard to interpret without per-scene distributions.

The contribution type is best read as Concept & Feasibility / Analysis rather than Algorithms/General; under that reading, the dataset and analysis protocol are the main artifacts, and their value would increase substantially if released alongside the paper (release is not clearly stated).

strengths: Addresses a genuine and timely gap: mechanistic interpretability of feed-forward 3D foundation models is largely unexplored, and VGGT is a high-impact subject model; this is among the first systematic causal analyses of geometric understanding in such a model.

The methodological design is sound and appropriately layered: probing across layers (correlational), QK attention analysis for correspondence structure (mechanistic), and attention-knockout interventions (causal). The supplementary strengthens this with progressively more localized interventions (whole map -> corresponding patches -> specific attention entries with softmax recomputation), which meaningfully mitigates the main confound of coarse knockouts.

The controlled synthetic ShapeNet/Blender dataset with complete ground truth (poses, correspondences, F/E matrices, multiple focal lengths and camera configurations) is well suited to the scientific question and enables clean splits including novel objects and symmetric/ambiguous assets.

The data-perspective experiments are informative beyond robustness benchmarking: the finding that VGGT partially 'hallucinates' occluded correspondences rather than ignoring them is an interesting, actionable observation about a widely used model.

Claims are generally carefully calibrated; the paper explicitly distinguishes correlation from causation and discusses residual confounds (e.g., heads may encode other mechanisms; SIFT's synthetic-data weakness confounding robustness comparisons). Limitations are honestly stated.
Reproducibility is reasonably supported: the model checkpoint is public, dataset construction is described in detail, and probing/intervention hyperparameters are provided.
weaknesses: Scale of evaluation is small in places: intervention results are averaged over only 5 scenes at a single focal length (50 mm), and several splits contain very few scenes (e.g., 5 novel-object scenes, 7 symmetric scenes). Some conclusions (e.g., the exact Sampson increase magnitudes in Figs. 4, 12-14) may not be robust; confidence intervals or more scenes would strengthen the causal claims.

The entire study is limited to two-view pairs of synthetic, largely textureless ShapeNet objects, while VGGT is a multi-view model trained on diverse real data. Generalization of the layer-wise findings (e.g., the layer 12-16 correspondence band) to real imagery and to >2 view inputs is unverified, which weakens the breadth of the conclusions.

The most localized intervention (Fig. 14) shows a much weaker effect (10.2 px) than whole-map knockouts (77+ px). While the paper reports this honestly, it leaves open how much of the large degradation in Figs. 4/12/13 is attributable specifically to correspondence matching versus broader disruption of those heads, so the headline causal claim is softer than the abstract suggests.

The robustness comparisons vs. SIFT+RANSAC are confounded by the synthetic, texture-poor data (acknowledged in Limitations), making the 'superior to classical pipelines' narrative partially circular; additional semi-real or textured scenes would help.

No comparison of the probed fundamental matrix against the F implied by VGGT's own predicted camera parameters, which would clarify whether epipolar structure in the tokens is consistent with the model's output geometry or partially redundant with pose information already encoded in camera/register tokens.

Relation to concurrent work (Stary et al. [25]) is mentioned only briefly; the specific overlapping findings and how this paper's contributions differ (beyond the model analyzed) deserve clearer delineation.
Fig. 3's per-head heatmap is dense and hard to read; several key numbers (e.g., probing details, additional splits) are deferred to the supplementary, reducing main-paper readability.

strengths: Timely and well-motivated research question: whether feed-forward 3D reconstruction foundation models (DUSt3R, VGGT, DA3) internally encode multi-view geometric principles or merely rely on learned priors. This addresses a genuine gap in interpretability of 3D vision models, as noted in the related work.

Methodologically systematic analysis combining complementary techniques: layer-wise probing of the fundamental matrix (a task never directly supervised, reducing confounding), QK attention-space correspondence matching analysis, targeted attention-knockout interventions with random early/late-layer baselines, and input-level perturbation experiments. The triangulation across these methods strengthens the causal narrative.

Good experimental controls and ablations: linear vs. MLP probes and 1-epoch probes to rule out probe overfitting (B.3), rank-2 singular value analysis as a second criterion (B.4), multi-view triplet probing (B.5), feature-similarity analysis as an alternative to QK attention (C.2, addressing the known caveat that attention can be misleading), DA3 model-size comparison (C.4), and multiple intervention locality levels (Whole heads/Image map/Block/Patch).

Breadth of evaluation: three architectures spanning different design paradigms (global vs. cross attention, camera tokens vs. averaged features), three real-world datasets plus a controlled synthetic ShapeNet dataset with complete ground truth, and semantic correspondence analysis on SPair71k revealing an interesting semantic-to-geometric transition in VGGT's layers.

Honest discussion of limitations: the authors explicitly acknowledge that the knockout experiments do not conclusively prove correspondence matching is solely responsible, note the hallucination-robustness trade-off under occlusion, and flag DUSt3R's frequent invalid pose predictions under intervention (72% of cases), reporting only valid cases.

Insightful and actionable findings: architecture determines where geometry emerges (middle layers for camera-token models vs. early layers for DUSt3R's asymmetric decoder), which could inform model design; the demonstration that VGGT exploits subtle lighting/shadow cues that classical pipelines miss is practically relevant.
weaknesses: Causal evidence has residual confounds: whole-head knockout removes all information carried by a head, not just correspondence matching, so the degradation could partly stem from disrupting other functions sharing those heads. The Patch-level interventions mitigate this (degradation shrinks substantially, e.g., 0.3px for DA3 in fig. 3), but this also weakens the strength of the 'causal link' claim in the abstract and contributions, which could be more carefully qualified.

Section 5 (role of learned priors) is noticeably weaker and less rigorous than Section 4: it is limited to VGGT only, quantitative results for scene perturbations (5.2) are largely deferred to the supplementary material, and the main-text presentation is mostly qualitative. The justification for restricting to VGGT is somewhat thin ('no clear indication of a fundamental difference'), and the occlusion experiment covers only 40 synthetic scenes at one focal length.

Statistical rigor is limited: results are reported as medians over very small test sets (e.g., 5 ShapeNet scenes for the attention analysis in 4.2), with no confidence intervals, variance estimates, or significance testing, making some between-model or between-condition comparisons hard to assess.

Novelty relative to prior work needs sharpening: Stary et al. [33] already analyzed a DUSt3R variant's layers and correspondences, and Han et al. [12] and Maggio et al. [22] probed VGGT internals. The main added value is the cross-model comparison and the intervention-based causal analysis, which is substantial but incremental in places; the paper could position its delta more explicitly.

The occlusion 'inpainting/hallucination' finding is under-analyzed: the connection to DINOv2's iBOT masking is only speculative, and it is not verified whether the inferred correspondences on occluded regions are geometrically correct (the authors themselves note hallucinations 'could be beneficial if correct' but never test correctness).

Synthetic dataset scope is narrow (single objects at the origin, object-centric, controlled renderings), and conclusions about real-world generalization rely on a limited set of real datasets; no code release or reproducibility statement is mentioned, which matters for a paper whose contribution is an analysis methodology.

No contribution type is declared; the work is best characterized as an Analysis/Concept & Feasibility contribution rather than a new algorithm. Judged under that lens the evidence is appropriate in kind, but several headline claims (e.g., 'causally linked' in the abstract) are stronger than the knock-out evidence strictly supports.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely question — whether feed-forward 3D reconstruction models (DUSt3R, VGGT, DA3) internally encode geometric structure or rely mainly on learned priors — and does so with a systematic, multi-model, multi-dataset design (three real-world datasets plus a controlled ShapeNet synthetic set with full ground truth).

The methodological pipeline is well-structured as an interpretability argument: probing for fundamental matrix recovery, QK-attention correspondence analysis, and attention-knockout interventions that provide causal (not merely correlational) evidence linking correspondence-matching heads to epipolar geometry encoding. The inclusion of random early/late-layer intervention baselines strengthens the causal claim.

Multiple robustness checks are included in the supplementary: linear probes and 1-epoch probes to rule out probe overfitting, rank-2/singular-value analysis as a second emergence criterion, triplet/multi-view probing, real-world correspondence-matching results mirroring the synthetic ones, and DA3 model-size comparisons.

The occlusion analysis is a genuinely interesting finding — the model retains ~50% of matching heads on occluded correspondences, suggesting inpainting-like behavior inherited from DINOv2's masked pretraining, which connects the geometric mechanism story to a concrete architectural source.

The learned-priors experiments (lighting/color, symmetric/repetitive scenes, focal length) against SIFT and SuperGlue baselines are well designed, and the honest observation that all methods fail under full geometric ambiguity shows the authors are not overclaiming.

The paper is candid about the limits of its causal claim (Section 4.3 acknowledges knockout effects do not conclusively prove correspondence matching alone causes epipolar encoding) and clearly distinguishes where architecture (global vs. cross-attention) shifts where the mechanism emerges.
weaknesses: Novelty is partially incremental. Stary et al. [33] already analyzed a DUSt3R variant and the role of layers/correspondences in multi-view transformers; the main novelty here is extension to three models, the knockout interventions, and the priors study. The paper does not sharply delineate its delta over [33], which weakens the contribution case.

The evidence for 'encoding epipolar geometry' is weaker than the framing suggests: probe Sampson errors are fairly large (roughly 5-40 px across models and datasets, and 26-45 px on MipNeRF360, which is why those results were relegated to the supplementary). Decodability of F is shown, but the recovered geometry is coarse; the abstract-level claim of emergent epipolar geometry could be tempered.

Potential circularity in the intervention evaluation: the fundamental matrix for Figure 3 is approximated from the model's own camera pose predictions, so any intervention that degrades pose estimation (for any reason, including general disruption of the layer) inflates the Sampson metric. The random-layer baselines partially control for this, but a metric based on held-out ground-truth correspondences or external F estimation would be more convincing.

Section 5 (learned priors) is restricted to VGGT with the justification that DA3 is 'not fundamentally different' — asserted rather than demonstrated. Key quantitative results for 5.2 appear only in the supplementary, leaving the main-text treatment thin relative to the paper's headline claims.

Some analyses rest on very small test sets (e.g., correspondence-matching evaluation over 5 scenes from 5 categories at a single 50 mm focal length), and the correspondence-matching metric (argmax attention hits the correct patch) is brittle; no confidence intervals or variance measures are reported.

The writing is uneven: DUSt3R's divergence in later layers is only 'speculated' to arise from independent target heads; Section 5's motivation jumps between questions; and Figures 2 and 12 are dense numeric heatmaps that are hard to read and arguably belong in the supplementary with summarized versions in the main text.

No mention of code or dataset release. Given that the contribution is an analysis (interpretability/analysis paper rather than a new algorithm), reproducibility of the probes, interventions, and the ShapeNet-based synthetic benchmark matters; absence of a release statement is a notable weakness.

The theoretical framing in Section 3.1 is textbook material that occupies space without adding to the argument, while methodological details that affect interpretation (e.g., why averaged decoder features for DUSt3R, how patch discretization ambiguities affect the accuracy metric) are deferred to the supplementary.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly posed research question: whether feed-forward 3D reconstruction foundation models internally encode multi-view geometry or merely rely on learned data priors — a question of genuine scientific interest to the community.

Methodologically sound and layered analysis: probing for the fundamental matrix (with linear-probe and single-epoch ablations ruling out probe overfitting), QK attention correspondence analysis, feature-similarity cross-checks (addressing the known unreliability of attention visualization), and targeted attention-knockout interventions establishing a causal link between correspondence heads and epipolar encoding. The progression from correlation to causal evidence is convincing.

Impressive breadth: three representative models (DUSt3R, VGGT, DA3) with architecturally distinct designs, three real-world datasets plus a controlled synthetic dataset with full ground truth, matched controlled comparisons (binned viewpoint differences), and multi-view (triplet) consistency checks.

The robustness study (occlusions, repetition/symmetry, lighting, focal length) yields a nuanced and honest conclusion — VGGT 'hallucinates' correspondences under occlusion and respects fundamental geometric limits under full symmetry — rather than an oversimplified story.

Emergence location differences (middle layers for camera-token models vs. early decoder blocks for DUSt3R, asymmetric vs. symmetric matching directions) provide architecture-interpretable insights that go beyond a single model case study.
Paper is well written, with take-away boxes per section and a thoughtful discussion acknowledging limitations of the causal interpretation (e.g., that the heads may encode additional mechanisms).
weaknesses: Section 5.2 (scene perturbations) is thin in the main text: it states conclusions qualitatively and defers all quantitative results (focal length, lighting/repetition experiments, figures 18-21) to the supplementary material. Given that 'the role of learned priors' is one of the two headline contributions, the main-paper evidence is disproportionately light, and no precise effect sizes for VGGT vs. baselines are presented in Section 5.2 itself.

Some experimental setups are narrow relative to the generality of the claims: the headline correspondence-matching analysis (Fig. 2) and the intervention study (Fig. 3) are run on only 5 scenes from 5 categories at a single focal length (50 mm) on the synthetic dataset; with only median statistics and no variance/interval estimates, the robustness of some head-level observations (e.g., 'top 4 heads in layer 14') is hard to judge.

For DUSt3R interventions, 72% of cases yield invalid camera poses and are excluded from the analysis, then marked with an asterisk in Fig. 3. This substantial selection effect weakens the comparability of the DUSt3R causal results and deserves more careful treatment in the main text.

The fundamental matrix is never directly supervised, but it is strongly determined by the supervised camera-pose/intrinsics heads, so the causal knockout is evaluated on a quantity (F derived from predicted poses) that is entangled with task-level supervision; the paper should discuss more explicitly whether the intervention disrupts correspondence computation or downstream pose aggregation.

Novelty positioning relative to the closest prior work (Stary et al. [33], which also studies layers and correspondences in multi-view transformers) is acknowledged but the delta could be articulated more sharply; several individual techniques (probing, attention knockout) are standard adaptations from NLP interpretability.

Figure legibility: several plots (Figs. 1-3, and dense numerical heatmaps in the appendix) are hard to read at print scale; the large numeric matrices in Figs. 2 and 12-15 would benefit from visualization rather than raw annotation.

The link between the occlusion-inpainting behavior and the DINOv2 iBOT masking loss is speculative and untested (e.g., no comparison against a VGGT variant without DINOv2 initialization), leaving the mechanistic explanation unverified.
